layer: L1-L6 / Python kernel package boundary and failure semantics
question: Now that graphrefly:D800 has Python own its kernel, where does that kernel live in the package, how do Python exceptions cross it, and what do the kernel conformance scenarios run against?
decision: (1) The kernel is the private package graphrefly._kernel: pure Python, typed, single-threaded, with no dependency on graphrefly._native or graphrefly-rs. It implements the kernel rules active by graphrefly:D798 and graphrefly:D799 and none of the draft module rules; it is not exported from graphrefly.__all__, and the public facade is its only package-level user. Sugar (the first-run gate of derived, effect and producer) lives in the facade, outside the kernel, and the docs call it Python sugar, not protocol. (2) The kernel catches Exception and nothing broader. An Exception from a node function or setup is that node's ERROR, its payload the exception object, which the facade surfaces as GraphCallbackError; an Exception from a sink callback goes to the host reporter, which the facade records as SubscriberCallbackError, and never becomes a node's ERROR; an Exception from a cleanup or from a queued request whose caller has returned goes to the host reporter. A BaseException that is not an Exception (KeyboardInterrupt, SystemExit, GeneratorExit and the like) propagates to the caller of the host call that was running, and becomes neither a node's ERROR nor a SubscriberCallbackError. Before it propagates, the kernel ends the interrupted request, drops the requests queued behind it and resets its in-wave state, without undoing arrays already delivered; the facade then poisons the graph as graphrefly:D436 requires, now without the native host-boundary abort path that graphrefly:D431 described. (3) The kernel scenarios are qualified by private tests in tests/kernel that drive graphrefly._kernel directly, in the ids and arrays the scenario text uses; this replaces graphrefly:D447's private native helpers. Facade behavior keeps its own tests, and graphrefly:D475's public-facade-first rule applies to facade-level checks. (4) The kernel has no awaitables: async work enters only at the facade's source, runner and adapter boundaries (graphrefly:D477, graphrefly:D480), whose results reach the kernel as ordinary later waves on the graph's owner thread.
rationale: graphrefly:D800 returns Python to a self-contained package and names graphrefly:D431, graphrefly:D436 and graphrefly:D447 among the decisions written only for the native boundary. Without that boundary, catching only Exception is enough to keep fatal BaseException out of graph ERROR and observer failures (the semantics graphrefly:D428 protects), and a private kernel package keeps the public facade the only public surface, as before. Scenario texts speak in node ids and arrays, which the kernel's own interface expresses directly; the public facade cannot send arbitrary arrays, by design.

completion.complete_when: graphrefly._kernel passes the kernel scenarios of graphrefly-py:D797-KERNEL-PY through tests/kernel, and the public facade runs on it with the failure semantics above.
completion.historical_when: A later decision moves the Python kernel or changes how exceptions cross it.

layer: L6 / Python public facade over the Python kernel
question: What public Python API does graphrefly expose once it runs on its own kernel under the D797 rules (graphrefly:D798, D799, D801, D802), with no compatibility layer?
decision: The package is pre-0.1 and keeps no shim, alias or old name (the user's choice of 2026-11-10). (1) Graph keeps state, producer, derived, effect, node, batch, describe, retain, reentry_queue, close and the context manager, and gains replace and definition. Graph.state(value=absent, name=None) returns State[T]; a state may start empty. Host input lives only on State: set(value) writes a value, set(callable) computes the value from the state's value when the write runs in request order (SENTINEL when there is none) and writes nothing when the callable returns its argument (is); a callable value is written wrapped (set(lambda _: f)); invalidate(), complete() and error(e) are the other three host inputs. A plain Node has no host write and no public down; Graph has no host input (Graph.invalidate, Graph.pause and Graph.resume go). (2) Graph.node(deps, callback, name=None, *, complete='auto', error='auto', invalidate='auto', quiet=False, setup=None, recipe=None) maps to the kernel node; partial, complete_when_deps_complete, error_when_deps_error, terminal_as_real_input, pausable, pull_id and restore go. Its callback runs on every wave it is given (no first-run gate); derived, effect and producer keep the first-run gate, documented as Python sugar, not protocol. setup(ctx) runs once per lifetime before the first run and may return the lifetime's cleanup. (3) Ctx keeps dep_len, has_data(i), data(i, default), wave_data, terminal(i), emit and state/has_state; wave_data lists each dependency's value arrays only (an INVALIDATE is no longer projected as SENTINEL), terminal(i) returns the dependency's COMPLETE or ERROR message of this run or None, and invalidated(i) reports an INVALIDATE under the manual policy. emit(*values) sends one array of DATA; down(*messages) sends one array of DataMessage, ErrorMessage and ControlMessage('INVALIDATE'/'COMPLETE') values, which the kernel checks; signal is the lifetime's abort signal (Signal, with aborted and on_abort); rewire(deps) changes the node's own dependencies for its lifetime. on_invalidate, on_deactivation, persist_state, request_pull, request_pull_next, pull, pull_params and rewire_next go, and with them PullContext and RewireNext. (4) Messages: subscribe and observe deliver one array per callback as a tuple of messages, the START array included. ControlMessage kinds are START, PENDING, RESOLVED, INVALIDATE and COMPLETE; ErrorMessage.error is a GraphCallbackError when a callback raised and otherwise the payload sent. Graph.observe delivers GraphEvent(path, messages, seq) per array a node publishes, without activating anything; GraphEvent loses tier. Node.status returns NodeStatus(cache, output, lifecycle), derived from what the node holds. Graph.describe returns the topology as data: each node's name, kind, current dependencies and quiet flag, with its value when it holds one. (5) Checkpoint: Graph.checkpoint() captures at a wave boundary (graphrefly._checkpoint, R-checkpoint) and restore_graph(checkpoint, *, registry) restores; a node is restorable when built with recipe=Recipe(ref, config), a JSON configuration; registry maps ref to a factory(config, RecipeContext) returning a callback, or a (callback, setup) pair; state nodes are always restorable. restore_ref, restore_registry, RestoreRef, RestoreDescriptor, RestoreContext and RestoreRegistry go. (6) A Subscription is released by unsubscribe, its context manager or Graph.close; dropping the handle releases nothing, since no finalizer owns release (as graphrefly:D527 and D557 have it for bundles). Graph(name, *, report=None) takes the host reporter for failures with no caller (a cleanup, a queued request, an observer); without one they are logged on the graphrefly logger. (7) The exception taxonomy (graphrefly:D428), the async runners and re-entry queue (graphrefly:D477, D480, D481), the network sources, Retain (graphrefly:D556) and the resource stack (graphrefly:D557) stay; the async and network sources lose their pausable argument.
rationale: graphrefly:D800 has Python own its kernel and keep its idiomatic facade where the rules allow; the cross-runtime alignment session settled the shared shapes with the user on 2026-11-10 (host input on State only, set folded with update as graphrefly:D797 does, one callback per array). The removed surfaces implemented rules D797 retired (PULL, PAUSE/RESUME, upward routing, per-run hooks, deferred rewire) or the native restore foundation that D800 retires; R-checkpoint (graphrefly:D802) replaces the descriptor-based restore with recipes.

completion.complete_when: The public facade runs on graphrefly._kernel with this API and its tests pass, with no graphrefly._native import.
completion.historical_when: A later decision changes the public facade.

layer: L6 / Python cross-graph facades during the deferred bridge phase
question: What happens to the public wire bridge facades when the facade moves onto the Python kernel while phase 6 (the bridge model) is deferred?
decision: Withdraw wire_bridge, wire_edge_group, wire_bridge_protobuf and wire_bridge_ack_driver, their bundles (WireBridge, WireEdgeGroup, WireBridgeProtobuf, WireBridgeAckDriver) and their status, issue and timeout types from the public package at the cut-over, together with the protobuf vector, WireEdgeGroup and mixed-locality tests that exercised the native bridge. Python claims none of C-1, C-1a, C-1b and C-1c until phase 6 brings the bridge back as Python code over the kernel, on the bridge model the root settles. The facade shapes of graphrefly:D516, D523, D524, D526, D527 and D542 are the starting point for that phase, not a public surface until then; graphrefly:D521's PyO3 classes go for good.
rationale: The user chose on 2026-11-10 to cut over after phase 5 instead of waiting for the deferred phase 6. The native bridge cannot attach to a graph that runs on the Python kernel, and it implements the two-phase DIRTY gate that R-graph-domain@2 replaced with a release grouped by cause, so it could not interoperate with migrated peers anyway.

completion.complete_when: Phase 6 of graphrefly-py:D797-KERNEL-PY restores the cross-graph facades on the Python bridge.
completion.historical_when: A later decision replaces this withdrawal.

decision: graphrefly is a pure-Python package built with hatchling from src/graphrefly and released as one universal py3-none-any wheel and an sdist for Python 3.12 and later. maturin, the PyO3 extension, the per-platform wheel matrix, the graphrefly-rs checkout in CI and release, and the graphrefly-rs cf02fc9 pin go. Development needs no Rust toolchain or sibling checkout; uv sync installs the package in editable form.

layer: L6 / Python node lookup by name
question: How does a host get a node it only knows by name, for example after restore_graph, and write it when it is a state?
decision: Graph.find(name) returns the node's own handle, or None when no node has that name; for a state node the handle is its State, so after a lookup or a restore the host writes it with set, invalidate, complete or error and narrows the result with isinstance. restore_graph builds every state node as a State handle. There is no separate narrowing method.
rationale: The cross-runtime alignment session settled on 2026-11-10, raised by Rust, that a lookup gives each node's own handle and a state's handle is its State in all three runtimes (Rust narrows with GraphNode::as_state). graphrefly-py:D4 left Python without a public lookup, so restored nodes were reachable only through private state.

completion.complete_when: Graph.find is public and restore_graph returns State handles for state nodes.
completion.historical_when: A later decision changes node lookup.

layer: L6 / Python wire bridge facades after graphrefly:D803
question: In what shape do the wire facades that graphrefly-py:D5 withdrew come back, now that graphrefly:D803 settles the bridge model (R-bridge@1)?
decision: The wire facades come back in the reference module's shape, in Python casing, with no shim for the old one. wire_edge_group_out(graph, *, group, edges, name) returns the node whose values are WireEdgeCause frames, one per sender wave in which an edge sent; frame_sink(send) is the subscribe callback that hands frames (or bytes) to a transport; frame_source(graph, open, *, name) is the receiving end, a node with no dependencies whose setup calls open(deliver); wire_edge_group_in(graph, *, group, frames, edges, name) returns WireEdgeGroupIn(gate, inbound, issues), whose gate releases a session's causes in order and at most once, reports gaps, drops stale causes and refuses bad frames whole, all as WireEdgeGroupIssue values. The envelope layer is wire_bridge(graph, *, session_id, outbound, received, max_attempts=2, name): numbered DATA envelopes over canonical protobuf bytes (outbound_bytes), acks of received DATA envelopes, frames and values that arrived (frames and values are quiet, so a wave that brought only an ack marks nothing), explicit ack-timeout ingress as a State (ack_timeouts) on which a pending attempt is sent again until max_attempts and then exhausted, and status and issues values; wire_bridge_ack_driver(graph, bridge, *, clock, timeout_ms, name) derives those facts from a clock node the host writes. Malformed bytes and facts are issues, never terminals; no timer is set. The canonical codec for WireBridgeEnvelope and WireEdgeCause is a strict hand-written private module (graphrefly._wire.protobuf) with no dependency; the public package exposes frames and bytes, not envelope values. Removed for good: the per-edge PENDING/DATA frames, one cause in flight, cohorts, tombstones, the drain, the edge group status node, wire_edge_group(inbound_edges/outbound_edges) and wire_bridge_protobuf.
rationale: graphrefly:D803 activates R-bridge@1 and names the reference module's wireEdgeGroupOut, wireEdgeGroupIn, frameSource and frameSink as the public shape for every runtime, and gives the envelope lanes the same shape (received envelopes from a source node, facts as state writes, outbound nodes with a transport sink). The alignment session asked on 2026-11-11 for the strict hand-written codec this session had recommended.

completion.complete_when: The wire facades pass C-1, C-1a, C-1b and C-1c on the Python kernel.
completion.historical_when: A later decision changes the wire facades.

layer: L6 / Python wire edge group gate after graphrefly:D804
question: How does the wire edge group gate treat arrays for an edge whose inbound node has already ended, now that graphrefly:D804 activates R-bridge@2?
decision: The gate of wire_edge_group_in skips the arrays of an edge whose inbound node has ended, in any frame, and releases the rest of the frame. When the skipped arrays do not end with a terminal, the sender's edge goes on while the receiver's has ended: the gate reports it as WireEdgeGroupIssue(kind="ended", session, cause, edge), a divergence only a new group repairs. A frame is still refused whole for an undeclared edge, a message that does not cross, a terminal that is not last in its array, or an array after its terminal in the same frame. The first cause of a session (wire_edge_group_out) puts an INVALIDATE ahead of every edge whose snapshot has no DATA, also an edge whose snapshot is its terminal alone, so a receiver drops a value an earlier session left. WireEdgeGroupIssue gains the kind "ended" and the field edge; the rest of graphrefly-py:D8 stands.
rationale: graphrefly:D804 activates R-bridge@2 and requalifies C-1b, answering the rule question this session raised on 2026-11-11: under R-bridge@1 a new session's first cause that repeated an ended edge was refused whole, so the INVALIDATE for every other edge was lost too.

completion.complete_when: The gate and the first cause follow R-bridge@2 and pass C-1b on the Python kernel.
completion.historical_when: A later decision changes the wire edge group gate.

question: Which Python exceptions are fatal at the kernel boundary, now that the D797 review found that a RecursionError from a long chain became one node's ERROR and left other nodes pending?
decision: RecursionError and MemoryError are fatal, as a BaseException that is not an Exception is under graphrefly-py:D2 (2): wherever the kernel or the facade would catch an Exception (a node function, setup, sink, cleanup, observer, signal listener, reporter or queued request), these two pass through; the kernel ends the interrupted request, drops the requests queued behind it and resets its in-wave state, and the facade poisons the graph. They are never a node's ERROR, a GraphCallbackError or a report. The rest of graphrefly-py:D2 stands.
rationale: The user chose on 2026-11-11, through the cross-runtime alignment session (D797 review Q15), that delivery and activation become iterative and that, at the least, Python treats RecursionError and MemoryError as fatal: after either, no node's state can be trusted, so turning one into the ERROR of whichever node was running breaks R-wave (each pending mark settles exactly once) and R-failure (a failure never enters an unrelated node's messages).

completion.complete_when: The kernel and facade let RecursionError and MemoryError pass as fatal and tests cover a function, a sink, a setup, a cleanup and a batch commit.
completion.historical_when: A later decision changes which exceptions are fatal.

layer: L6 / Python facade failures, definitions, recipes and set after the D797 review
question: How do the facade's failure reporting, Graph.definition, recipe factories and State.set work, after the D797 review found a kept failure history, a stale definition, a recipe context without make, and set(fn) relying on is and callable()?
decision: (1) A subscribe or observe callback that raises an Exception goes, wrapped as SubscriberCallbackError (graphrefly:D428), to the kernel, which gives it to Graph(report=...) or, without a reporter, to the graphrefly logger; nothing keeps it. Subscription.callback_errors and the on_error argument of subscribe and observe go. (2) Graph.definition(node) reads the callback and setup from the instance the kernel holds, so a replace that a throwing batch body dropped or the kernel refused when it ran leaves them as they were. (3) RecipeContext is (graph, name, make), where make(ref, config, name) builds another registered recipe and returns its (callback, setup). (4) State.set takes an updater only when the value is a function, a method or a functools.partial; a class or an object with __call__ is written as a value. An updater writes nothing when it returns the value it was given: the same object, or an equal value of the same type among bool, int, float, str and bytes, where NaN is the same as NaN and -0.0 is not 0.0 (Python's reading of Object.is in R-request-order). (5) A ctx stays usable in a cleanup that Graph.close runs. The rest of graphrefly-py:D2 and graphrefly-py:D4 stands.
rationale: The two D797 reviews (graphrefly sessions/active/REVIEW-D797-migration-fable.md 2.6, 2.14, 2.17 and REVIEW-D797-migration-codex.md F11) found these against R-failure@3 (the host reporter is a callback and the kernel keeps no failure history), R-node@2 (the current definition), R-checkpoint@1 (a factory is given a way to build another registered recipe), R-request-order@2 (Object.is) and R-lifetime@2 (a cleanup may still read the private state). The user chose (review Q9) that without a reporter failures go to the graphrefly logger and with one only to it. SubscriberCallbackError stays because graphrefly:D428 names it and the user asked to keep that taxonomy; only where it goes changes.

completion.complete_when: The facade reports subscriber and observer failures, reads definitions from the kernel, gives recipe factories make, applies the set definitions above, and its tests cover each.
completion.historical_when: A later decision changes these facade behaviors.

layer: L6 / Python public messages and ctx reads after the D797 review
question: What shape do public messages and a node callback's input reads take, now that the D797 review asked all three runtimes to share the rule's shapes (review Q3 and Q11)?
decision: (1) A public message is a tuple whose first element is its type, as the rule, the kernel, the checkpoint and TS have it: (DATA, value), (ERROR, error) and (START,), (PENDING,), (RESOLVED,), (INVALIDATE,), (COMPLETE,). graphrefly exports the seven type constants START, PENDING, DATA, RESOLVED, INVALIDATE, COMPLETE and ERROR, whose values are those strings. DataMessage, ErrorMessage and ControlMessage stay only as type aliases of those tuple shapes, for annotations; the dataclasses go. subscribe and observe deliver one array per callback as a tuple of message tuples, and GraphEvent.messages is one. (2) Ctx.down(array) takes one array, a list of message tuples, and the kernel checks it; varargs go. Ctx.emit(*values) stays and sends exactly one array per call. (3) ctx.deps[i] is the only input read, a Dep view with id (the dependency's name), waves, terminal (its COMPLETE or ERROR tuple of this invocation, or None), has, value (the latest value, or graphrefly.SENTINEL without one, since None is valid DATA under graphrefly:D428) and invalidated (under the manual INVALIDATE policy); Dep is exported. dep_len, has_data(i), data(i, default), wave_data, terminal(i) and invalidated(i) go, with no alias. The rest of graphrefly-py:D4 stands, including Graph.node with no first-run gate and derived, effect and producer with theirs.
rationale: The user chose on 2026-11-11, through the cross-runtime alignment session (D797 review Q3, Q4 and Q11), that every runtime gives the rule's ctx.deps[i] view with no second per-index API, that emit sends exactly one array per call, and that Python's public messages return to tuples, with ctx.down taking a list. The package is pre-1.0 and keeps no shim.

completion.complete_when: The facade delivers tuple messages, Ctx has deps, emit and down(list) and no per-index reads, and its tests and docs use them.
completion.historical_when: A later decision changes public messages or ctx reads.

layer: L4 / Python graph layer under R-graph-surface@1
question: How does the Python facade take the graph layer that graphrefly:D805 activates as R-graph-surface@1 (find, describe, observe, retain)?
decision: (1) Graph.find(node_id, /) gives the node with that id, a state node as its State, or None, and activates nothing. (2) Graph.describe() gives a list with exactly {'id', 'kind', 'deps', 'quiet'} per node, in creation order, deps current (a ctx.rewire's included); the graph's name, has_value and value are gone, and values and status are read from the node. (3) Graph.observe(nodes, callback) subscribes to each node as an ordinary subscriber, so it activates a cold node and keeps it active, and calls callback with one GraphEvent(id, msgs) per delivered array, START first, PENDING and the kernel's RESOLVED included, with no sequence number; GraphEvent's path, messages and seq fields go. The passive kernel hook graphrefly._kernel.Graph.observe and its observer list are removed. (4) Graph.retain(node) is a subscriber that ignores what it receives; each call is its own subscription. Both observe and retain return a Subscription: unsubscribe() is the rule's stop and release, idempotent, also a context manager, and closed by Graph.close like any subscription. The Retain class and its export, retain's reason argument and the graph lifetime's retained-subscription bookkeeping are removed; the lifetime keeps a plain list for the wire bridges it closes.
rationale: graphrefly:D805 activated R-graph-surface@1 on 2026-11-11, and the cross-runtime alignment session asked graphrefly-py to adopt it (the user's choices for Q6 of the D797 migration reviews). In Python the stop or release is the Subscription handle that Node.subscribe already returns, so observe and retain give the same idempotent, thread-checked handle that Graph.close also closes, rather than a bare function. A separate Retain type added nothing once a retain is an ordinary subscription. The package stays below 1.0 and keeps no alias for removed names (graphrefly-py:D4, graphrefly-py:D13).

completion.complete_when: find, describe, observe and retain have these shapes, the kernel has no observe hook, Retain is gone and C-48 has a facade test.
completion.historical_when: A later root decision revises R-graph-surface.

layer: L4 / Python subscription handle under R-graph-surface@1
question: What do subscribe, observe and retain return in Python, given that every runtime should share one shape for the stop and the release?
decision: (1) The shared shape: Node.subscribe, Graph.observe and Graph.retain return a Subscription that is called to stop, stop(); calling it again does nothing, and once it is called nothing more is delivered to the callback, also when it is called during a wave. This is the shape TS gives as () => void and Rust as FnOnce(). (2) Python extensions on the same object: a with block stops it on exit, and .closed says whether it has stopped; Graph.close() stops every one of them. (3) Subscription.unsubscribe() is removed, with no alias. This replaces the clause of graphrefly-py:D15 under which unsubscribe() is the stop and the release; the rest of graphrefly-py:D15 stands.
rationale: The user decided through the cross-runtime alignment session on 2026-11-11 that the three runtimes use one shape, a function to call, and that each language's own features come as extensions on top of it. A Python object with __call__ is that function and can still carry the with block and closed, which other Python code expects. The package stays below 1.0 and keeps no alias for removed names (graphrefly-py:D4, graphrefly-py:D13).

completion.complete_when: subscribe, observe and retain return a callable Subscription without unsubscribe, a stop during a wave delivers nothing more, and the docs and tests call stop().
completion.historical_when: A later decision changes the subscription handle.

layer: L4 / when a Python stop takes effect
question: When does the stop that subscribe, observe and retain return take effect, given that graphrefly-py:D16 said nothing more is delivered once it is called, also during a wave?
decision: (1) The stop of Node.subscribe and of Graph.retain is an unsubscribe request (R-request-order, C-33): called during a wave, it waits until the wave ends, so the wave's remaining arrays, a second array of the same run included, are still delivered to that callback, and nothing is delivered after the wave ends. (2) The stop of Graph.observe takes effect at once: nothing more is handed on after it is called, also during a wave (R-graph-surface@1); its subscriptions are released when the wave ends. (3) .closed says whether stop() has been called. This replaces the clause of graphrefly-py:D16 under which nothing more is delivered once any stop is called; the rest of graphrefly-py:D16 stands.
rationale: The cross-runtime alignment session corrected on 2026-11-11 what it had passed on for graphrefly-py:D16: R-request-order makes a subscribe or unsubscribe asked for during a wave wait until the wave ends, C-33 says so for an unsubscribe asked for during an invocation, and the reference kernel and graphrefly-rs (its C-33 test) deliver the rest of the wave. R-graph-surface@1 says of observe that nothing more is handed on after its stop.

completion.complete_when: A subscribe stopped during a wave still gets that wave's remaining arrays and nothing after it, a retain released during a wave is gone when it ends, and observe hands on nothing after its stop.
completion.historical_when: A later root decision changes when an unsubscribe or an observe stop takes effect.
